title: South Africa’s commodity price index fell in dollars and rose in rand in October
summary: South Africa’s commodity price index moved in opposite directions depending on the currency used to measure it. The 10 November SARB release put October’s dollar-denominated commodity price index at 282.0, down 0.5% from 283.5 in September. In rand, the index rose 1.7%, from 363.1 to 369.1. Both use 2015 as the reference year. The difference is directly relevant to exporters whose revenue is earned at world prices and whose expenses include rand wages and services. It does not establish their realised margins, since actual sales volumes, contract prices, hedges and imported input costs also matter.

Figure 2 shows iron ore and gold as the largest negative weighted contributions in October, closely followed by palladium and platinum. Brent crude and coal provided the two largest positive offsets. Platinum-group metals themselves were divided: rhodium contributed negatively, while iridium and ruthenium contributed positively. These bars measure contributions to the headline monthly change, so they do not rank the commodities by their individual price returns. Table 1 poses a separate question about index construction. The dollar index excluding gold rose 0.5%, while the index excluding all platinum-group metals fell 1.9%. The release does not give the weights or a bridge between the exclusion series and the headline. It is therefore possible to identify the largest offsets in the published figure without assigning the 1.4 percentage point gap between the headline and ex-PGM readings to a single metal.

The annual comparison tells a second story. Dollar commodity prices were still 20.8% above October 2025, but twelve-month growth slowed from 26.4% in September. The rand index was up 15.7% year on year, down from 17.3%. Table 1 shows the dollar index had already fallen sharply in June and only partly recovered by September. Monthly direction, annual growth and the cumulative change from an earlier peak therefore answer different questions. An export-income estimate based on October’s annual growth rate would not be a measure of the latest monthly impulse.

Measured in the two currencies, the change in October implies an approximate ratio of 1.017 divided by 0.995, or about 2.2%, using the rounded growth rates. This is a way to describe the translation wedge between the two index returns, not an observed daily exchange-rate move or a precise estimate of exporters’ exchange rates. The release offers a dated export-price indicator. It supplies no announcement-day asset response, national-accounts volume estimate or estimate of the resulting tax receipts.

questions.question: How are the exclusion indices reconciled to the headline basket?
questions.detail: Figure 2 identifies the main positive and negative contributions. It leaves open why the ex-PGM index fell further than the headline despite negative contributions from several prominent PGMs. Start with the September Quarterly Bulletin methodology cited in footnote 1, the component weights and unrounded series. Reproducing the exclusion indices would determine how well either series represents an exporter’s particular metals exposure.

questions.question: How much of the rand revenue gain was actually realised by exporters?
questions.detail: Compare the currency translation in the index with contract invoicing dates, export volumes and hedging where disclosed. Distinguish dollar prices at the reference date from the exchange rates used to convert receipts in company accounts. A rand-denominated index gain could coexist with falling earnings if quantities declined or local costs rose faster.

questions.question: Did the softer dollar index meaningfully change the external or fiscal outlook?
questions.detail: Match the relevant product categories to recorded export values, royalties and tax payments, allowing for shipment lags and the profitability thresholds of different producers. The large year-on-year index gain and small monthly fall apply to different horizons. Neither alone establishes the direction of the latest change in the trade balance or government revenue. Observe whether any estimated response survives alternative export weights and contemporaneous exchange-rate adjustments.
